quote: Man soll durch eine endliche Zahl von Operationen entscheiden, [-...-] ob in irgend einer Reihe $(\beta)$ eine 0 vorkommt [-ob-] oder ob alle Reihen $(\beta)$ nur Einsen bestehen?
english: One is to decide by a finite number of operations whether a 0 occurs in any sequence (β), or whether all sequences (β) consist only of ones?
topic: After notes on simplifying a proof (using a definite-integral formula or Schlömilch's Compendium), Hilbert formulates every mathematical problem as deciding, by finitely many operations, whether a rule-generated 0-1 sequence ever contains a 0, and claims that every mathematical problem is solvable.

triage.modern_statement: Hilbert describes a family of 0-1 sequences (β), each produced by a finite rule. The question is whether there is a uniform procedure that takes such a rule and decides, in finitely many steps, whether a 0 ever appears or whether every term is 1. In modern terms the rule is a computable (or primitive recursive) function f: N -> {0,1}, and the question is whether the Π1 statement '∀n f(n)=1' is decidable. That is the same as asking whether a program ever halts by finding a 0. Hilbert's claim that every mathematical problem can be reduced to this form and is solvable is his 'non ignorabimus' axiom of solvability, which later became the Entscheidungsproblem / decision-problem program.
triage.answered_by: The general claim was refuted in the negative. Gödel's incompleteness theorem (1931) showed that no complete, computable axiomatization of arithmetic exists, so some Π1 statements of this kind can be neither proved nor refuted. Church and Turing, independently in 1936, proved the Entscheidungsproblem unsolvable. Turing's paper is 'On computable numbers, with an application to the Entscheidungsproblem', Proc. London Math. Soc. 2(42), 1936. The undecidability of the halting problem, which is commonly credited to Turing's paper but was not stated there in exactly that form, shows directly that no algorithm can decide whether a rule-generated 0-1 sequence contains a 0. Later, Hilbert's 10th problem was also shown to be unsolvable (Matiyasevich, building on Davis, Putnam and Robinson, 1970).

evidence.claim: In his 1900 Paris lecture Hilbert stated his conviction that every mathematical problem can be solved ('in mathematics there is no ignorabimus').

Historical analysis of Hilbert's 'axiom of solvability' (every mathematical problem can be settled by a finite number of operations) and how it turned into formal decidability and the decision problem.

Gödel (1931) showed there is no complete, computable axiomatization of first-order arithmetic. Church and Turing independently proved the Entscheidungsproblem unsolvable, and Turing proved related unsolvability results.

Turing 1936, 'On computable numbers, with an application to the Entscheidungsproblem', is the usual citation for the undecidability of the halting problem. Whether that attribution is accurate is itself debated.
Hilbert's 1900 conviction that every problem has an answer reachable in finitely many steps is contrasted with the unsolvability of Hilbert's 10th problem.

triage.why: Hilbert's general version, a uniform finite procedure that decides for every rule-generated 0-1 sequence whether it contains a 0, is exactly the decision problem for Π1 sentences, which is equivalent to the halting problem. Church and Turing showed in 1936 that this cannot be done, and Gödel's 1931 result already showed that no complete formal system settles all such statements. The idea itself is the well-known 'non ignorabimus' / axiom-of-solvability thesis from Hilbert's 1900 Paris address. It is not one of the 23 problems as such, but it is the core of the later Entscheidungsproblem, which has been settled negatively. Computability theory is still an active field, but this specific question is closed. The one interpretive uncertainty is whether Hilbert meant a single uniform method or that each individual problem can be settled. Either way, the 1931 and 1936 results refute the claim as a general principle.
